content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends rapid drug susceptibility testing (DST) for isoniazid and rifampicin, or rifampicin alone, at the time of tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis. This approach is preferred over conventional testing or no testing, depending on resource availability. For monitoring patients undergoing treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), the use of sputum smear microscopy combined with culture is recommended over sputum smear microscopy alone. Anti-tuberculosis (anti-TB) drugs are categorized into groups based on their efficacy, clinical experience, and drug class. First-line anti-TB drugs are included in Group 1, except for streptomycin, which is classified with other injectable agents in Group 2. Drugs in Groups 2–5, excluding streptomycin, are considered second-line or reserve drugs. Cross-resistance is a significant concern, as resistance mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis to one drug may lead to resistance to other drugs within the same family or, less commonly, to drugs in different groups. For MDR-TB treatment, WHO guidelines strongly recommend the use of fluoroquinolones and ethionamide (or prothionamide), despite the evidence being of very low quality. Later-generation fluoroquinolones are preferred over earlier-generation ones. Treatment regimens should include at least four second-line drugs likely to be effective, including a parenteral agent, along with pyrazinamide during the intensive phase. Additionally, regimens should include pyrazinamide, a fluoroquinolone, a parenteral agent, ethionamide (or prothionamide), and either cycloserine or para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) if cycloserine cannot be used. Major updates to second-line anti-TB regimens for MDR-TB include the recommendation to use at least four effective second-line drugs during the intensive phase. There is no evidence supporting the use of more than four second-line drugs, even in cases of extensive disease. Ethambutol and Group 5 drugs may be used but are not part of the standard regimen. In cases of culture-negative pulmonary tuberculosis, the inability to isolate M. tuberculosis does not rule out active TB. Alternative diagnoses should be considered, and further diagnostic studies should be conducted. A diagnosis of TB can be inferred from clinical and radiographic improvement following anti-TB treatment. Reevaluation after two months of therapy is essential to assess treatment response. If improvement is observed and no other cause is identified, treatment should continue. Standard regimens include six months of therapy or a combination of isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RIF), pyrazinamide (PZA), and ethambutol (EMB) for two months, followed by INH and RIF for an additional two months. HIV-infected patients with culture-negative TB should be treated for at least six months. For individuals with radiographic evidence of prior TB and a positive tuberculin skin test, but without adequate prior therapy, sputum examination and further evaluation are recommended to rule out active TB. If active TB is excluded, treatment for latent TB infection should follow standard regimens. In pregnant women, TB treatment should begin if the likelihood of maternal disease is moderate to high. The initial regimen should include INH, RIF, and EMB, as these drugs cross the placenta but are not teratogenic. Streptomycin, however, is contraindicated due to its association with congenital deafness. PZA is likely safe during pregnancy and is recommended by WHO and the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (IUATLD). If PZA is excluded, therapy should last at least nine months. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated for women on first-line anti-TB drugs, as the drug concentrations in breast milk are minimal and non-toxic to the infant. However, these drugs in breast milk are not sufficient to treat TB or latent TB in the infant. Pregnant or breastfeeding women taking INH should receive pyridoxine supplementation (25 mg/day) to prevent peripheral neuropathy. In low-income countries, TB control faces challenges due to the rise in HIV infections, neglect of TB programs, and the emergence of drug-resistant strains. WHO declared TB a global health emergency in 1993 and developed the Stop TB Partnership to save millions of lives. Treatment strategies in high-incidence, low-income countries differ from those in low-incidence, high-income countries due to resource limitations. WHO and IUATLD guidelines emphasize the DOTS strategy, which includes government commitment, case detection via sputum smear microscopy, standardized treatment regimens, uninterrupted drug supply, and a standardized recording system. WHO and IUATLD recommend an eight-month regimen for patients with relapsed, interrupted, or failed treatment. Chronic cases, likely caused by MDR organisms, require susceptibility testing and tailored second-line regimens if resources permit. Recent pharmacological advances include the FDA approval of bedaquiline in 2012 for MDR-TB and extensively drug-resistant TB. Bedaquiline targets the ATP synthase proton pump, differing from quinolones, which target DNA gyrase. However, it carries a black-box warning for arrhythmias and potential cardiac arrest. A novel three-drug regimen (PaMZ) combining PA-824, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide has shown promise, achieving significant bacterial reduction within two weeks in clinical trials. Research priorities in TB treatment include developing drugs to shorten and simplify treatment for drug-susceptible TB, improving therapies for drug-resistant TB, and enhancing treatment for latent TB infection. Promising drug classes include nitroimidazopyrans and oxazolidinones. Experimental data suggest that targeting isocitrate lyase, an enzyme essential for latent TB, may be effective. Other potential interventions include novel drug delivery systems, cytokine modulation, and nutritional supplementation. Research is also needed to identify factors predicting relapse risk and adherence to therapy, enabling more efficient resource allocation and treatment supervision.
